title: Using the MySQL SOURCE Command to Import a SQL File
description: SOURCE vs the < redirect — when to use each, why SOURCE sometimes fails on big files, and how to see errors instead of silent stops.
author: SQLSplit

content.text: SOURCE runs a SQL file from inside the MySQL prompt. It's handy when you're already connected, but it behaves differently from the shell redirect — and that difference bites people on large imports.

content.title: Use an absolute path, no quotes
content.text: SOURCE doesn't understand ~ for your home directory and doesn't want quotes around the path. /Users/you/dump.sql works; "~/dump.sql" does not.
For very large dumps, the shell redirect is usually the safer choice — it streams the file rather than loading it through the interactive client:

If SOURCE returns to the prompt instantly with no error and no data, the path is wrong — MySQL couldn't open the file. Double-check the absolute path and that the file is readable by the user running mysql.
See errors instead of silent stops
By default a single bad statement aborts the import. To push through recoverable errors (useful for messy dumps), start mysql with --force:
Redirecting STDERR to a log file gives you a list of exactly which statements failed, instead of guessing.

content.title: Big dump dying mid-SOURCE?
content.text: Split it into smaller files and SOURCE them in order — each one is independently importable.

faq.question: What's the difference between SOURCE and mysql < file.sql?
faq.answer: SOURCE runs from inside the mysql prompt; the < redirect runs from your shell. For very large files the shell redirect streams more efficiently, while SOURCE is convenient when you're already connected interactively.

faq.question: Why does MySQL SOURCE say 'No such file or directory'?
faq.answer: SOURCE needs an absolute path with no quotes and no ~ shortcut. Use the full path like /Users/you/dump.sql and make sure the file is readable by the OS user running the mysql client.

faq.question: How do I make MySQL continue importing after an error?
faq.answer: Start the client with --force so it skips failed statements instead of aborting. Redirect STDERR to a log file (2> errors.log) to capture exactly which statements failed.
